Pearl Avenue runs past the high-school lot, Bends with the trolley tracks, and stops, cut off Before it has a chance to go two blocks, At Colonel McComsky Plaza. Berth’s Garage Is on the corner facing west, and there, Most days, you'll find Flick Webb, who helps Berth out. Flick stands tall among the idiot pumps— Five on a side, the old bubble-head style, Their rubber elbows hanging loose and low. One’s nostrils are two S’s, and his eyes An E and O. And one is squat, without A head at all—more of a football type. Once Flick played for the high-school team, the Wizards. He was good: in fact, the best. In ’46 He bucketed three hundred ninety points, A county record still. The ball loved Flick. I saw him rack up thirty-eight or forty In one home game. His hands were like wild birds. He never learned a trade, he just sells gas, Checks oil, and changes flats. Once in a while, As a gag, he dribbles an inner tube, But most of us remember anyway. His hands are fine and nervous on the lug wrench. It makes no difference to the lug wrench, though. Off work, he hangs around Mae’s Luncheonette. Grease-gray and kind of coiled, he plays pinball, Smokes those thin cigars, nurses lemon phosphates. Flick seldom says a word to Mae, just nods Beyond her face toward bright applauding tiers Of Necco Wafers, Nibs, and Juju Beads.

Positioned on the westward-facing corner sits Berth's Garage, and that's where you'll usually spot Flick Webb, who works there as Berth's assistant.

Flick towers over the mindless gas pumps, which stand five in a row in that outdated round-topped design, their flexible rubber hoses dangling limply. # Flick Webb: A Life After Glory

Flick Webb works at Berth's Garage on Pearl Avenue, where he earns his living performing the routine tasks of an ordinary service station attendant. His days are filled with pumping gas, checking oil, and changing flat tires—a modest existence marked by physical labor and repetition.

Yet Flick's present circumstances stand in stark contrast to his celebrated youth. In high school, he was an exceptional basketball star for the Wizards, a genuine local hero whose talent set him apart. In 1946, he established a county record of 390 points, an achievement so remarkable that it still stands to this day. On the court, Flick possessed a grace and skill that promised a bright future.

However, that promise was never fulfilled. Despite his extraordinary athletic gifts, Flick never learned a trade or developed the practical skills needed to build a stable career. Now, he performs menial work that goes largely unnoticed and unappreciated. This lack of recognition is poignantly symbolized by the indifferent lug wrench—a tool that, unlike the cheering crowds of his youth, offers no applause or admiration for his efforts.

After his workday ends, Flick drifts through his evenings with little purpose. He spends his time idly at Mae's Luncheonette, where he plays pinball, smokes cigars, and drinks lemon phosphates. These small diversions fill the hours but reveal a life lacking direction or meaning, a man going through the motions without any real sense of fulfillment.

Ultimately, the poem draws a powerful contrast between Flick's glorious past and his empty present. His moment of greatness has long since faded, leaving behind a diminished life that never lived up to its early potential. Through Flick's story, the poem reflects on the fleeting nature of youthful success and the quiet tragedy of a life that peaked too soon.

# Ex-Basketball Player: A Study in Faded Glory

John Updike's poem "Ex-Basketball Player" offers a haunting portrait of Flick Webb, a man whose life peaked before it truly began. Once a celebrated high-school basketball star, Flick set a county scoring record that seemed to promise a bright and limitless future. Now, however, he spends his days pumping gas at Berth's Garage, his remarkable talents reduced to menial labor and his youthful promise long forgotten by the town that once cheered his name.

Updike constructs this contrast through richly evocative imagery and skillful personification. The poem opens by describing the road that leads into town—a road that "runs past the high-school lot" and seems to slow down, "bends with the trolley tracks, and stops, cut off / Before it has a chance to go two blocks." This description of the truncated street subtly mirrors Flick's own interrupted journey, a life that stalled before it could reach its potential. At the garage, Updike famously personifies the gas pumps, describing them as standing "Like idiot pumps" with their rubber elbows hanging loose, an image that reflects both the mechanical monotony of Flick's work and the wasted grace of hands that once handled a basketball with extraordinary skill.

Indeed, it is Flick's hands that most poignantly evoke his lost brilliance. Updike writes that Flick's "hands were like wild birds," a simile that captures the natural, almost supernatural talent he once possessed on the court. Yet these same hands now perform the dull tasks of checking oil and pumping gas. When Flick occasionally picks up an inner tube and dribbles an air hose, we glimpse a flicker of his former self—a fleeting, almost pathetic gesture toward a glory that will never return.

The tragedy of Flick's situation lies not in dramatic downfall but in quiet, unremarkable diminishment. He drifts through an aimless adult existence, sometimes loitering at Mae's luncheonette, where he sits beneath the "bright applauding tiers / Of Necco Wafers, Nibs, and Juju Beads." This final image is especially cutting: the rows of colorful candies stand in for the cheering crowds that once celebrated his triumphs, but now they offer only silent, meaningless decoration. The applause of his youth has been replaced by the indifferent packaging of a roadside diner.

Through Flick Webb, Updike delivers a moving meditation on the fleeting nature of athletic fame and the danger of achieving one's greatest moments too early in life. Flick's story is a cautionary tale about lost potential—a reminder that early success, when it fails to translate into lasting purpose, can leave a person stranded and unfulfilled. The poem asks us to consider what happens to those who shine brightly in youth only to find themselves forgotten, their talents unused and their futures foreclosed. In its gentle yet unflinching portrayal of a life defined by what it once was rather than what it might become, "Ex-Basketball Player" resonates as a universal reflection on the emptiness that can follow the fading of the spotlight.

# Pearl Avenue

Down where the city softens into quiet neighborhoods, there runs a street unlike any other. Pearl Avenue earned its name honestly—residents say that on misty mornings, the pavement seems to shimmer with a soft, opalescent glow, as if the road itself were carved from a single strand of jewels.

What makes Pearl Avenue truly memorable, however, is the way it moves. Rather than cutting a straight, predictable line through the district, the street bends and curves like a lazy river finding its path. Each turn reveals something new: a corner bakery with steamed windows, an old oak leaning over a garden wall, a bookshop tucked into the crook of a gentle bend.

Newcomers often lose their way among these winding stretches. "Just follow Pearl until it bends left past the fountain," locals will tell you, "then keep going where it bends again by the blue house." The directions sound simple, but the avenue has a personality all its own, twisting according to some logic older than the map.

Photographers love the golden hour here, when sunlight pools in the curves and the shadows stretch long across the cobblestones. Couples stroll arm in arm, following the bends without hurry, letting the street decide their pace.

There is a lesson in Pearl Avenue, some might say. The straightest road is rarely the most beautiful. Sometimes the greatest treasures—like pearls themselves—are found only by those willing to follow the gentle, unexpected turns of the journey.

# Glory Days at Pump Number Three

He fills the tank on aisle two,
the fluorescent buzzing overhead,
and somewhere in his memory
the crowd still roars instead.

'89, the county finals—
forty points, the buzzer beat.
They carried him on shoulders then
down Main Street's frozen sleet.

The trophy's somewhere in a box,
the newspaper turned brown,
his jersey number '22'
now just a fading crown.

"You played ball, right?" a stranger asks,
recognizing something old.
He nods and rings the coffee up,
the story left untold.

At night he shoots at the driveway hoop,
the same old rusted rim,
and for a moment, forty-eight,
the boy comes back to him.

The ball still finds the bottom
with that soft familiar sound—
proof that some things in this life
stay true when he comes around.

He locks the station up at ten,
the highway humming low,
not every star burns out from failing—
some just choose to slow.

And maybe glory isn't gold,
or crowds that scream your name,
but knowing how to love a thing
long after leaves the game.

**Glory Days on Route 9**

Danny Kowalski pumps gas now,
the same station where he used to
lean against the Coca-Cola machine
after Friday night games,
his letterman jacket heavy
with the weight of everyone's Saturdays.

You should have seen him then—
the way the whole town emptied
into those aluminum bleachers,
how the stadium lights turned
ordinary boys to bronze,
and Danny, number twelve,
running like the future
was something you could catch.

Now he wipes his hands
on a grease-stained rag,
watches the cars pull through,
their drivers barely nodding,
strangers who never saw him
split two defenders in the rain,
the ball tucked like a promise
against his ribs.

Across the street, Meyer's Luncheonette
still spins its counter stools,
still serves the same egg creams
in the same fogged glasses,
and sometimes Danny goes in
for coffee, black, no sugar,
sits where he sat at seventeen
when the world was a scholarship
just waiting to be signed.

The candy display by the register—
Bit-O-Honey, Necco Wafers,
Mary Janes in their yellow wrappers—
hasn't changed in twenty years,
and neither, he thinks,
has anything that mattered,
except the way time folds
a person's best days
into the back pocket
of a fading town.

He remembers the knee,
the crack that echoed
louder than the crowd,
how the doctors spoke
in careful voices,
how the recruiters stopped
returning calls,
how the trophies grew a skin of dust
on his mother's mantle.

Outside, the gas pumps click
their steady numbers,
the price of moving on,
and Danny leans again
against the machine,
older now, and heavier,
watching the road that leaves
this place, that carried others
somewhere else,

while the sun goes down
behind the water tower,
that rusting crown
above a kingdom
of one traffic light,
one diner,
one man
still running
in a memory
nobody else remembers
anymore.
